sections.h2: What makes selling a house in St. Petersburg different?
sections.html:
Waterfront geography, storm repairs and permit history decide how quickly a St. Petersburg house can close. The city occupies a peninsula in Pinellas County, and its website describes 244 miles of shoreline along Tampa Bay, Boca Ciega Bay, the Gulf of Mexico and intracoastal waterways.

That coast helps with pricing and complicates disclosure. Buyers, lenders and insurers ask whether the property lies in a flood hazard area, whether past storm damage was fixed under permit, and what the city has on file. Gather those answers early and you can say yes to a strong offer quickly, whether it comes from a listing or a cash buyer.

sections.h2: What does St. Petersburg look like for a home seller?
sections.html:
The city reports more than 265,000 residents across over 100 neighborhoods and calls itself one of the nation's fastest-growing cities. Its history page says the town of St. Petersburg incorporated on February 29, 1892, and re-incorporated as a city in 1903.

The city's own profile helps explain neighborhood demand:

  • A seven-mile preserved downtown waterfront and 137 parks and recreation areas.
  • The Pinellas Trail, a 54-mile route running coast to coast.
  • St Petersburg College, Eckerd College, USF St. Petersburg and Stetson University College of Law.
  • Averages of 74 degrees and 361 days of sunshine a year, per the city.

Proximity to the waterfront, the Pier and downtown arts venues can move prices block by block, so compare your house with sales from your own neighborhood rather than the citywide picture.

sections.h2: What should I check with the St. Petersburg building department?
sections.html:
Start with permit history and flood records, both held by the city's Construction Services and Permitting Division at the Municipal Services Center, One 4th St. N. The city says homeowners should get permits before repair, improvement or construction begins.

Florida House Bill 803, effective July 1, 2026, lets the city issue a Permit Exemption form for work on a single-family dwelling totaling less than $7,500. The city says this applies only outside flood hazard areas and does not cover structural components (including window, door, roofing, soffit and siding work), mechanical, electrical, plumbing or gas work.

City certificate types listed by the St. Petersburg permitting office
CertificateWhen the city says it is needed
Certificate of OccupancyNew construction, change of use, combining units, rebuilding after condemnation or fire
Temporary Certificate of OccupancyNew construction delayed on a non life-safety item, once major trades have a partial final
Certificate of CompletionFinished work that does not need a CO; required for a building shell, otherwise optional
Elevation CertificateFEMA document showing height above sea level and base flood elevation; city records go back to 1990

The city also lets you research Certificate of Occupancy history for free in its property cards database. Pull yours before you list.

Bring a photo ID and a floor layout if you visit in person. The city also offers an optional preliminary plan review for proposed work, a useful step if a buyer wants to add to the house after closing.

sections.h2: How does flood and storm history affect a St. Petersburg sale?
sections.html:
If your house is in a flood hazard area and was damaged, the repair path matters to the sale. The city's permitting page points owners to FEMA's 49% Rule, which can affect a property after storm damage, and asks homeowners to bring photos, a damage summary and a floor layout when they visit.

The Pinellas County Property Appraiser notes a related tax effect: when a structure is damaged or destroyed, taxes can still rise for long-time homesteaded owners because of the Save Our Homes cap recapture rule. If the building value fell below land value, the assessed value may not drop.

  • Keep storm photos, adjuster reports and repair invoices together.
  • Locate any elevation certificate on file with the city for your address.
  • Confirm every repair that needed a permit has a final inspection.
  • Ask the buyer's insurer early about flood coverage, since it can change the closing timeline.

Cash buyers often purchase storm-damaged houses as they are, but expect a discount tied to the unknowns.

The Pinellas County Property Appraiser also advises owners with storm-damaged structures to read the value reconsideration letters they receive, since a building value can differ from the one used the year before.

sections.h2: How are Pinellas County property taxes handled when I sell?
sections.html:
The Pinellas County Property Appraiser values your home each January 1, and the Pinellas County Tax Collector sends the bill in November. A sale is a change of ownership, so the county says exemptions and caps the prior owner held come off on the next January 1, and the buyer's value resets toward market.

The homestead exemption of up to $50,000 requires a March 1 application. Florida's printed early-payment discount runs from 4 percent in November down to 1 percent in February. Ask your closing agent how the current year's taxes will be prorated.

If the buyer is moving from another Florida homestead, portability may carry over a savings cap. That is the buyer's application to file, within three years of January 1 of the year the earlier homestead was left.

sections.h2: What do deed and recording charges look like in St. Petersburg?
sections.html:
Pinellas deeds carry Florida documentary stamp tax at 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, which the clerk takes at recording. The Department of Revenue states that every party to the document is liable, regardless of the contract's allocation.

Recording itself costs $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 per added page under statute 28.24, with further per-page charges. A title company lists each item on the settlement statement.

Cash offers often skip lender steps like appraisals, which may shorten the schedule. Still, ask who covers title insurance, stamp tax and tax proration, and get the split in writing before accepting.

sections.h2: How do I verify contractors and open permits in St. Petersburg?
sections.html:
The city's permitting page tells homeowners to hire a licensed contractor and points to the Pinellas County Licensing Board for checking a contractor's license. It also says difficulty scheduling an inspection can come from an unknown license status, which shows how closely the system ties permits to licenses.

For work still in progress, the city's online portal lets you enter a permit number to schedule or cancel an inspection and check plan review status trade by trade. For e-plan submittals, applicants get ten business days to finish uploads or answer comments before the application is denied and the workflow ends.

  • Look up each contractor on the county licensing board's site.
  • Enter permit numbers in the city portal to see open reviews.
  • Call the permitting division at 727-893-7231 for license status questions.

A buyer's inspector will usually find stalled work, so settle it first or disclose it.

faqs.q: Where do I get permit records for a St. Petersburg house?
faqs.a: Ask the city's Construction Services and Permitting Division at One 4th St. N. The city also offers a free property cards database for researching Certificate of Occupancy history, and its online portal tracks permit status.

faqs.q: Do small repairs in St. Petersburg need a permit?
faqs.a: Not always. Since July 1, 2026, a form lets the city exempt single-family work under $7,500 outside flood hazard areas, but not structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing or gas work. Confirm with the building department before starting.

faqs.q: Does my Save Our Homes cap go to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. A sale resets the assessment to just value on the next January 1, so the buyer's tax bill can be much higher than yours. The buyer can apply for a new homestead exemption by March 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a storm-damaged house in St. Petersburg as is?
faqs.a: Yes. Many buyers purchase as-is, but disclose known damage and any unpermitted repairs. If your property is in a flood hazard area, ask the city about FEMA's 49% Rule before you decide to repair or sell.

faqs.q: What population does the city of St. Petersburg report?
faqs.a: More than 265,000 people, across over 100 distinct neighborhoods, according to the city's own profile page. Use the latest Census Bureau estimate if you need an official count.
